cases.title: On 9x9, Black takes a White stone in the corner by filling its last liberty.
cases.notes: The source runs the same shape on 13x13 too; left out because LiGo launches with 9x9 and 19x19 only (R-SCOPE-1).

cases.title: On 19x19, Black takes a White stone in the corner by filling its last liberty.
cases.notes: The source runs the same shape on 13x13 too; left out because LiGo launches with 9x9 and 19x19 only (R-SCOPE-1).

cases.title: Black's corner stone has no empty neighbour of its own but takes two separate White stones at once, so it is legal.
cases.notes: Also covers GoLegalityTest.scala:126 (the same placement, asked as a legality question). No ko point: two stones came off.

cases.title: Each side captures one stone in a ko; both prisoner counts are still there after the two passes that start scoring.
cases.notes: Combines the source's 'accumulate' (:48) and 'survive the passes' (:51) checks. Its settlement and score checks (:54, :58) are not imported: strategygames' settlement and area score are not used by LiGo (R-SCORE-3).

cases.title: White surrounds a two-stone Black chain and removes it; the two emptied points can be played again.
cases.notes: The source also counts 71 legal placements; the format has no count field, so the two freed points are checked instead.

cases.title: Neither player may place a stone on a point that already holds one, whoever's stone it is.
White may not play into the corner point that Black's two stones surround, because it would capture nothing and have no liberty.
Black may not fill the last liberty of its own two-stone chain, even though the new stone touches a friendly stone.
On 9x9, Black takes one stone in a ko; White may not take back at once.
cases.notes: Also covers GoLegalityTest.scala:61-73 (same position on 9x9).

cases.title: On 19x19, Black takes one stone in a ko; White may not take back at once.
cases.notes: The source runs the shape on 13x13 too; left out (R-SCOPE-1).

cases.title: After one move each elsewhere, White may take the ko back.
White takes the ko back; now the ko point is where Black's stone was, and Black may not take back at once.
On 19x19 near the bottom edge, White takes a ko; Black may not take back at once.
Black passes instead; the ko point is cleared and White may fill the ko.
cases.notes: The source also counts 353 and 354 legal placements; the format has no count field.

cases.title: Black captures a lone White stone; White may not play back into the hole, because that is suicide (not ko).
cases.notes: PlayStrategy issue #489 regression. Same sequence as GoSituationTest.scala:313. The source's 76 placements are 77 empty points minus this suicide point.

cases.title: After White passes, Black may fill the point its capture emptied.
cases.notes: PlayStrategy issue #489 regression (GoSituationTest.scala:340 too).

cases.title: White captures one stone but its capturing stone joins a larger chain, so there is no ko and Black may capture back at once (snapback).
Black's snapback removes White's whole three-stone chain.
Right after White takes one stone, Black takes two stones back on the same point; this is not a ko recapture and is legal.
cases.notes: PlayStrategy issue #490 regression. Same sequence as GoSituationTest.scala:348.

cases.title: Sending two, returning one: Black gives up two stones and would retake one, but that would repeat an earlier position, so it is refused and play goes on.
A move that captures nothing but would recreate the position of six moves earlier, same player to move, is refused.
White takes a ko, both players pass, Black resumes play: the immediate retake is still refused, because passing does not lift a superko ban.
cases.notes: In strategygames two passes do not stop play, so its test retakes straight after them; LiGo has a scoring phase in between, so a resume was added (R-SP-6). The refused retake repeats a situation after a stone placement, so it does not depend on open point 1.

cases.title: A capture that brings back an earlier board but with the other player to move is allowed (situational, not positional, superko).
After that capture the board is exactly as three moves earlier, the game goes on, and it is Black's turn.
In a triple ko, the move that would bring back the same position with the same player to move is refused; the game is not ended or voided.
In the corner, a capture that brings back an earlier board with the other player to move is allowed.
A ko retake that would repeat an earlier position is refused, also when a pass was played earlier in the fight.
Two passes at the very start end play and start the scoring phase.
cases.notes: strategygames keeps offering placements after two passes (source :46); in LiGo a placement needs a resume first (R-SP-1, R-SP-6), see sg-resume-then-stone-back-to-play.

cases.title: A single pass does not end play; it is simply the other player's turn.
After some play, a pass by each player ends play and starts the scoring phase.
cases.notes: The source's settlement checks (:73-:95) are not imported: dead stones are agreed in lila's scoring phase, not by strategygames' settlement (spec §9).

cases.title: Both pass, play is resumed, and Black (whose turn it naturally is) places a stone: the game is back in play.
cases.notes: In strategygames a placement after two passes simply closes dead-stone selection; LiGo needs an explicit resume (R-SP-6), which was added.

cases.title: Pass, pass, resume, White plays a stone, pass, pass: the scoring phase starts again (the passes before the stone do not count twice).
cases.notes: Also GoSituationTest.scala:417. The source plays the stone straight after two passes; LiGo needs a resume first, added here. Resuming again is allowed because a stone was placed since the previous resumption (R-SP-9). During the scoring phase neither a stone nor a pass may be played (R-SP-1): strategygames would accept both (a placement just closes dead-stone selection, GoEndingTest.scala:52; a third pass is allowed, :62), so the adapter must refuse them.

cases.title: Four passes around a resume do not end the game with no dead stones: a new scoring phase starts, and a second resume with no stone played since the first is refused.
cases.notes: Inverts the source on purpose: strategygames settles the game with no dead stones on the fourth pass (passesSettlingTheGame = 4); the spec says that must never happen (§9, §10 'infinite games'). The adapter owns this (unit 1.7). Also GoSituationTest.scala:394.

cases.title: A 2-stone handicap on 9x9 puts Black's stones on the fixed star points and gives White the first move.
cases.notes: strategygames' only handicap test covers 4 stones on 9x9 (GoHandicapTest.scala:31), so this case takes its board from strategygames' handicap table; the table row equals spec R-HCP-4. The 1-stone row is deliberately not imported: the spec overrides it (R-HCP-2).

cases.title: In a 4-stone game White answers in the corner; the handicap stones stay and it is Black's turn.
A 2-stone game on 9x9: White starts, the players alternate, and two passes start the scoring phase with the board unchanged.
cases.notes: The source walks the recorded FENs of this game from a 2-stone start; the expected board is its FEN after the second pass (:197).

cases.title: Black fills the last liberty of a White stone in the corner and takes it.
One Black stone fills the shared last liberty of two separate White stones and takes both.
Same position with White to move: White may play the shared point, which captures nothing.
cases.notes: The source asks whether White's placement would capture its own stones (it must not); a legality check is the closest thing the format can state.

cases.title: Black's stone touches one White chain on two sides and removes all three of its stones (counted once).
Black may not play into a corner point enclosed by two separate White stones.
Black may not join its stone in the corner if that takes the whole chain's last liberty.
A Black corner stone with no liberty of its own is legal because it captures the White stone next to it; that makes a ko, so White may not take back at once.
cases.notes: The source checks the capture only. The ko point and the refused retake are added from R-KO-4 and R-KO-2: the retake would recreate the starting situation, which counts for superko.
